newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Record VAT receipts swell UK public purse.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Record VAT receipts swell UK public purse.

text.p: The British government collected 3.875 billion pounds ($6.2 billion) more in tax than it spent on public services last month as value-added tax (VAT) receipts chalked up a record high.
The Office for National Statistics said VAT receipts of 5.032 billion pounds was the highest monthly total since records began and outstripped the 3.783 billion collected in the same month last year.
As a result, July's debt repayment was well above the 929 million pounds paid back in July last year, even though the privatisation proceeds column was blank for the first time in months.
City economists, who had forecast a more modest repayment of 1.9 billion pounds, said the bumper crop of VAT returns was indicative of the frantic pace of high street spending.
"The headline is an amazingly good figure," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident. "It certainly ties in with the very strong state of the economy."
That will give the Bank of England cause for concern despite its pledge to call a halt to the recent succession of interest rate rises for a while, in order to take stock of the economy.
Monday's figures left financial markets on tenterhooks until Wednesday when the latest snapshot of high street activity, in the form of July retail sales figures, is released.
The FTSE index of 100 leading shares was helped by the data and recouped some of its early dramatic losses. It was 24 points lower at 4,842 around midday amid fears of further losses on Wall Street.
But gilts, British government bonds, posted healthy gains. The less debt the government has the fewer gilts it has to issue and, according to the laws of supply and demand, gilt prices should rise.
"The figures suggest the government will be able to meet this year's borrowing requirement (forecast) without any real problems," said Jeremy Hawkins, economic adviser at BankAmerica.
"This is clearly very positive from the supply side for gilts." A

key question for the monetary authorities is what proportion of a tidal wave of free shares from building societies converting into banks -- 36 billion pounds at the last count -- is being spent rather than saved.
Investment bank Robert Fleming conducted a poll of 3,000 people with market researchers Mintel and on Monday said it expected about a quarter to be spent, boosting economic growth by 0.5 percent.

As for Monday's figures, income tax receipts totalling 8.18 billion pounds, versus 7.32 billion in July last year, and corporation tax of 3.91 billion pounds, up 14 percent year-on-year, showed the broad-based strength of the economy.
"VAT receipts rebounded particular sharply. But other forms of receipts were also strong," said Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets.

The latest figures also showed the government is keeping public spending under tight control. Net departmental outlays totalled 21.59 billion pounds last month, compared with 21.54 billion in July last year.
"Departmental outlays up just 0.2 percent year-on-year suggests that the impressive spending restraint seen in the second half of last year continues," Loynes said.
The government has pencilled in a 10.9 billion pounds public sector borrowing requirement for the 1997/98 financial year. That could now be undercut, he said.
